doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Marshall Stearns's Friday record sessions at Yale
summary: Avakian describes Stearns's collection and open house, and labelling records with Jerry King.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You had mentioned Marshall Stearns as a very important person in your life.

Absolutely. Marshall Stearns was a graduate school student. We all thought he was a college professor because he had a byline that gave 20 Lake Place, New Haven, Connecticut as the place to write to him about questions about jazz and so forth. But to my surprise when I enrolled as a freshman in 1937 I found that he was living just off campus with his wife and going to the graduate school to get a Ph.D. in English Literature. And the great discovery was that Marshall not only had a superb record collection but he had an open house every Friday night for anyone who wanted to come and listen to records and talk and exchange ideas. So having been invited to come anytime, for the two years that it took for Marshall to finish up his Ph.D., I was in his home almost every Friday night, mainly with a classmate named Jerry King, who was also an enthusiastic young collector. And we heard the whole history of jazz really in that great collection he had, which filled I would say five rather wide shelves, and it was carefully catalogued and the collection ended up at the Rutgers Institute of Jazz ‘cause Marshall wanted to establish a center for study, research and so forth, and that’s what he chose to do. And as I go through the collection of 78s, I quickly recognize on the corner of these heavy green paper jackets the writing on the labels, the clear handwriting is mine and the not-so-easy-to-read handwriting is Jerry’s. But he called us all brownies, because whenever he had a number of review records to go through, he kept the ones that he © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
wanted of course and he asked us to make out the labels, and so that’s how it came about that there are two years worth of labels made out by King and Avakian.
